title: A wave from many sources
sub: Rotting Oranges, 01 Matrix and Pacific Atlantic: every source in the queue at once, and searching back from the borders
cards/0/title: The problem: rot spreads from everywhere at once
cards/0/body:
Rotting Oranges (LeetCode #994). An m×n grid, up to 10×10: 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange, 2 is a rotten one. Every minute a rotten orange infects its fresh side neighbors. After how many minutes are no fresh oranges left? If some orange will never be reached, return −1.

Signals: “every minute — to the neighbors” and “minimum time” mean level-order BFS from u10.l1: one level of the queue is one minute, and the level size is queue.Count at its start. Only one thing is new: there is more than one source. The rot spreads from all rotten oranges at once, and an orange rots in the minute the nearest wave reaches it.

In other words, the minute an orange rots is its distance to the nearest rotten orange (through fresh cells), and the answer is the largest of these distances.
cards/1/body:
The same problem in its pure form is 01 Matrix (LeetCode #542): in a matrix of 0s and 1s (m·n ≤ 10⁴, at least one 0), find for every cell the distance to the nearest zero in side steps.

Naive: launch a BFS from every one and stop at the first zero — BFS yields cells in order of distance, so the first zero is the nearest. One BFS is up to m·n cells, there are up to m·n ones, O((m·n)²) in total. The same goes for the oranges: a BFS from every fresh orange to the nearest rotten one, or a simulation that scans the whole grid every minute — and there can be up to m·n minutes (oranges in a snake corridor), a square again.

The repeated work is plain to see: neighboring cells have answers that differ by at most 1, yet every BFS walks almost the same territory all over again.
cards/2/q: 01 Matrix at 100×100: a single zero in a corner, ones everywhere else. How much work does the naive “BFS from every one to the first zero” do, and what follows?
cards/2/options/0: ≈ 10⁸ cells: from far-away ones the BFS covers almost the whole grid — right at the time limit, and the work is repeated
cards/2/options/1: ≈ 10⁴: each BFS finds a zero within a few steps
cards/2/options/2: ≈ 2·10⁶: each BFS only walks to the corner, at most 200 steps
cards/2/explain: There are 10⁴ − 1 ones. A BFS from a cell at distance d from the corner visits every cell closer than d — thousands of cells for the far half, about 0.7·10⁸ dequeues in total, and several times more counting the neighbor checks. At 10⁸ operations per second that's a second or more — all for answers that differ by 1 between neighbors.
cards/2/wrong/1: There is one zero, and it's in the corner. Far cells are up to 198 steps from it, and on the way the BFS covers everything closer — thousands of cells.
cards/2/wrong/2: The path to the corner is up to 198 steps long, but BFS doesn't walk a path: it visits every cell closer than the zero, because the wave expands in all directions instead of heading to the target.
cards/3/title: The key idea: every source goes into the queue at once
cards/3/body:
Turn the question around: not “where is the nearest source for this cell” but “how far does the wave from all sources reach”. Put all sources into the queue with distance 0 and run one BFS. It is the same as a BFS from an imaginary vertex connected to every source: each cell is claimed by the wave that arrives first, that is, from the nearest source.

Invariant: the queue holds cells at distance d followed by cells at d + 1, never anything else. So a cell's distance is final the moment it is first reached — mark on push, as in lesson 1. Each cell enters the queue once: O(m·n) instead of a square.

Oranges. The sources are the rotten oranges, a level is a minute, and the fresh counter tracks fresh ones. The loop runs while there is a queue and fresh oranges: after the level on which the last fresh orange rots, the queue isn't empty — it holds the last rotten ones — and without the fresh > 0 condition the loop would take one more level, infect nobody and add a minute. If the queue runs out while fresh > 0, someone can't be reached: the answer is −1. No fresh oranges at the start — the loop never runs, the answer is 0.
cards/4/explain: Every rotten orange goes into the queue up front — that is the multi-source BFS. The loop lives while fresh oranges remain: otherwise an extra level adds a minute. The level size is taken from queue.Count before the loop. An infected neighbor becomes 2 when it is pushed, so nobody pushes it twice. If fresh oranges remain, the answer is −1.
cards/5/task: Step through the trace on a 4×5 grid with rotten oranges in two corners. One rig step is one minute, that is, one BFS level; the oranges that rotted during that minute are circled. The rig will ask twice what happens next.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: Minute 1: (1, 0), (0, 1), (2, 4) and (3, 3) rotted. How many oranges will rot in minute 2?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: The next level is the fresh neighbors of these four: (1, 1), (0, 2), (2, 3) and (3, 2). (1, 1) is adjacent to both (1, 0) and (0, 1), but it rots once: (1, 0) meets it first and paints it 2, so for (0, 1) it is no longer fresh. Marking on push keeps it from being counted twice.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: Minute 4 infected nobody: one fresh orange is left, (0, 4). The queue is empty. What does the code return?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: The side neighbors of (0, 4) are (0, 3) and (1, 4), both empty; (1, 3) is diagonal. The wave can't cross empty cells, the queue is exhausted, and fresh = 1 — the answer is −1. The problem asks when all of them rot, so an unreachable orange can't just be dropped.
cards/6/body:
In 01 Matrix the sources are all the zeros. Put them in the queue with distance 0 and give the ones −1, “not known yet”. No separate visited is needed: −1 is the mark. Pop a cell, and every neighbor with −1 gets a distance one larger and joins the queue. The distance is set once, on push, and never changes: waves that arrive later won't be any closer.

There's no need to separate levels here: the distance is stored in the cell itself. Each cell enters the queue once — O(m·n) time and memory.

In a game this is a distance map: for every cell, how many steps to the nearest exit, cover or enemy. An agent that always steps to a neighbor with a smaller number reaches the nearest target without any pathfinding. Flow fields are built on this (u12.l4).
cards/7/task: Step through 01 Matrix on a 4×5 grid with three zeros. A cell shows the distance found so far, “?” means not known yet; below is the queue. The rig will ask twice what the code does.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Push nothing: the neighbors already have distances
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Give (3, 1) a 2 and push it again
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Overwrite (3, 1) with 1: (3, 0) is closer to a zero
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: We pop (3, 0) at distance 1. What does the code do?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: The neighbor above, (2, 0), is a zero. The neighbor to the right, (3, 1), got a 2 when (2, 1) was popped — before (3, 0). The dist != −1 check filters out both. There's nothing to overwrite: (3, 0) and (2, 1) are both at distance 1, so the wave from either gives that cell a 2, and (3, 1) can't have a 1 — it isn't next to a zero.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Nothing new: no unknown cells are left, the maximum is 2
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: The queue holds 9 cells at distance 2. What will this level produce?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: Count them: 3 zeros, 8 cells at distance 1 and 9 at distance 2 — all 20 cells. The “?” marks vanished from the grid when these 9 cells were pushed, because distance is set on push. Level 2 will only check neighbors and won't find a single −1. (0, 0) is two steps from the zero at (2, 0), and (1, 2) is two from (0, 3).
cards/8/q: On the grid [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] the code returns 5, but the answer is 4. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/8/explain: In minute 4 the last orange, (2, 2), rots and joins the queue. The loop sees a non-empty queue and takes one more level: (2, 2) infects nobody, but minutes++ still runs — 5. It needs while (queue.Count > 0 && fresh > 0). “Subtract one at the end” breaks another case: on a grid without a single orange the answer is 0, and you'd get −1.
cards/9/title: Pacific Atlantic: search from the borders, not from the cells
cards/9/body:
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow (LeetCode #417). A height map m×n, up to 200×200. The Pacific touches the top and left edges, the Atlantic the bottom and right. Rain flows from a cell to a neighbor that is not higher. Find the cells from which water reaches both oceans.

Naive: from every cell, a “downhill” traversal and a check whether it touched both oceans — O((m·n)²), up to 1.6·10⁹ for 200×200.

Reverse search. Water from cell X reaches an ocean ⇔ you can climb from the ocean to X stepping against the flow: into a neighbor not lower than the current cell. The sources are all the cells on the ocean's edge — once again a single multi-source traversal per ocean. Two traversals give two maps, “drains to the Pacific” and “drains to the Atlantic”, and the answer is the cells marked in both. O(m·n).

The same reversal works whenever the question is “from every cell to one of the targets”: search from the targets. Surrounded Regions (#130) and Number of Closed Islands (#1254) are solved by a traversal from the border: whatever it reaches is connected to the border.
cards/10/q: The reverse traversal from the Pacific stands on a cell of height 5. Its right neighbor has height 3 and isn't marked yet. Will the traversal go there?
cards/10/options/0: No: water from the 3 won't flow into the 5, so the 3 doesn't drain to the ocean through this cell
cards/10/options/1: Yes: water flows downhill, from 5 to 3
cards/10/options/2: Yes: the traversal marks every neighbor, and heights are compared at the end, when the maps are intersected
cards/10/explain: The traversal runs against the flow: it answers “where can water come here from”. Water can come into the 5 only from a cell no lower than 5. The 3 may well drain to the ocean, but by another route — if so, the traversal will reach it from there.
cards/10/wrong/1: Water does flow from 5 to 3, but that's the direction from the cell to the ocean. The reverse traversal starts at the ocean, so it moves toward the water.
cards/10/wrong/2: Without the height check on each step the traversal marks the whole map: every cell is connected to the edge. The “not lower” condition is the whole point of the problem.
cards/11/title: Unity: influence maps and the basis of flow fields
cards/11/body:
Multi-source BFS is a workhorse of grid-based game AI. From all enemies you get a threat map: how many steps to the nearest enemy; a unit retreats to the neighbor with a larger number. From all exits, an evacuation map: a thousand agents step to the neighbor with a smaller number and reach the nearest exit. One BFS in O(cells) serves every agent at once, while A* per agent means a thousand separate searches. This is the basis of flow fields (u12.l4).

In practice. A 256×256 map is 65,536 cells and about 2.6·10⁵ neighbor checks per rebuild. Keep the dist array and an int[] queue of w·h cells (each enters once) in fields — no garbage. Rebuild when the sources move or every few frames, not in every Update.

Where BFS stops working. If cells cost different amounts (swamp 3, road 1), queue levels no longer equal distance: you need Dijkstra (u12.l1). If a diagonal step costs the same as a side step, BFS over eight neighbors still works.
cards/11/deep:
Why 01 Matrix isn't just “two DP passes”. There is also a queue-free solution: a pass from top-left to bottom-right and a reverse pass, dist = min(dist, neighbor + 1). It is correct on a grid without walls — a shortest path there can always be split into two monotone pieces. With walls (a level map) the path winds around, two passes aren't enough, while BFS works on any graph.

Jobs and Burst. BFS is sequential, but it can move off the main thread: an IJob with NativeArray<int> for dist and the queue, and Burst usually speeds such loops up noticeably. While the job computes the new map, agents read the old one — double buffering, as in Game of Life from u3.l5.

Influence, not distance. An “influence map” in strategy games is often a sum of contributions with falloff (enemy strength divided by distance, propagation with a per-step factor). That is no longer a minimum over sources, and a single BFS can't produce it: it is computed by propagation with decay across the grid, or by adding up maps per group. The BFS distance map is the special, cheapest case.

Partial updates. If one source moves, only cells whose distance could change need updating. For BFS maps it is simpler to rebuild the whole thing, but large worlds split the map into chunks and rebuild only those the wave of changes passed through.
cards/12/q: You are solving Rotting Oranges out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: side neighbors, what to return if there are no fresh oranges at the start and if one is unreachable
cards/12/items/1: Naive: a BFS from every fresh orange to the nearest rotten one — O((m·n)²)
cards/12/items/2: Idea: all rotten oranges in the queue at once, one BFS, a level is a minute
cards/12/items/3: Code: fresh counts the fresh ones, mark on push, loop while there's a queue and fresh > 0
cards/12/items/4: Run the example minute by minute, check an orange with two rotten neighbors
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: no fresh oranges — 0, a fresh orange cut off by empty cells — −1
cards/12/explain: First agree on the edge answers (0 and −1) — the loop condition depends on them. Then the naive baseline, the multi-source BFS idea, the code with its two traps (the extra minute and double counting), the run-through and the cost.
cards/13/q: Match the problem to the technique.
cards/13/pairs/0/0: After how many minutes all oranges rot
cards/13/pairs/0/1: All rotten in the queue, a level is a minute
cards/13/pairs/1/1: BFS from all zeros, dist set on push
cards/13/pairs/2/0: Cells from which water reaches both oceans
cards/13/pairs/2/1: Two traversals against the flow from the edges
cards/13/pairs/3/0: A fresh orange cut off by empty cells
cards/13/pairs/4/0: A thousand agents head for the nearest exit
cards/13/pairs/4/1: One distance map from the exits
cards/13/pairs/5/0: A swamp costs more than a road
